rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient spanning nearly the full solvent range at mid temperature to reveal the overall retention window and whether any compounds are strongly retained or bunched. This should maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds in one run and give a balanced first map for later optimization.

All compounds were already baseline-resolved, so the only clear improvement path is lowering the time penalty. A longer gradient at the same composition range and temperature should spread the crowded mid-region around peaks 5–7 while still keeping all 10 compounds comfortably within the 42 min window.

Resolution is already perfect, so we should reduce analysis time by making the gradient slightly stronger at the start while keeping the same endpoint and gradient time. Raising phi0 should pull the early and mid eluters forward and may improve CRF if the minimum resolution stays above the threshold.

The last change improved CRF by shortening the run without harming resolution, so the next logical step is to further increase starting strength. This tests whether we can compress the chromatogram more and gain time while keeping the current critical pair comfortably resolved.

CRF has improved monotonically as phi0 increased, and the minimum resolution remains comfortably above 1.5, so pushing phi0 one more step is the most efficient way to seek a faster run. This should test how close we can get to the resolution limit while trimming additional time from the last peak.

The trend is still favorable: increasing phi0 keeps shortening the run, and the critical pair remains above the 1.5 threshold, though it is tightening. One more step should locate whether the optimum is still at higher phi0 or whether we are about to cross the resolution limit.

phi0 = 0.20 is currently the best compromise: at 0.25 resolution breaks down, so the optimum likely lies near the 0.20 boundary with a slightly shorter gradient. Reducing tG by one step may improve time further while checking whether the critical pair around peaks 6–7 still stays above the resolution threshold.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the best use of the next run is to probe whether an even shorter gradient can maintain it and define the robustness boundary. Shortening tG one more step should show whether the critical pair near peaks 6–7 drops below acceptable resolution or if the optimum plateau extends further.

The optimum appears centered near phi0 0.20 and tG 18, with the critical pair just safely above the limit, so now it is worth testing whether a slightly lower phi1 can compress the late empty portion without hurting separation. This explores whether the broad 0.95 endpoint is more than needed, while staying close to the proven max-CRF conditions.

Since changing phi1 did not help, the best-known composition-time point remains injection 7; the remaining useful axis to probe is temperature. A small increase in T may shorten retention enough to preserve the zero time penalty while revealing whether selectivity around the critical 6–7 pair improves or worsens.

Higher temperature strongly worsened the critical selectivity, so the informative opposite test is a lower temperature around the current optimum method. This checks whether cooler conditions increase the 6–7 resolution while potentially retaining the zero time penalty and could identify a more robust max-CRF region than 40 C.

The central optimum is already known, so a different useful probe is to extend the temperature trend further to define how sharply selectivity collapses on the hot side. This can help map robustness and confirm that 40 C is the unique viable maximum-CRF region.

The hot-side trend is nonmonotonic but still suboptimal, so one more step to 55 C will complete the temperature map and define robustness limits around the known optimum. This is a high-information run because it can show whether the selectivity loss around the critical pair continues, recovers, or shifts to a new pair.

The temperature optimum is clearly centered at 40 C, but the cold side has only been sampled at 35 C where selectivity changed abruptly. Testing 30 C completes the opposite edge of the temperature map and may reveal whether the 35 C failure was a local inversion or part of a broader trend.

With temperature and phi1 mapped, the remaining local robustness axis around the optimum is phi0. Dropping phi0 one step from the max-CRF method should test whether the optimum is a narrow edge at 0.20 or whether there is a broader robust plateau with extra resolution margin at essentially no score cost.

The optimum method is already established, so the most informative unused setting nearby is the final hot-end temperature. Running 60 C completes the temperature survey and fully brackets robustness around the winning method.

The endpoint has only been tested at 0.90 versus 0.95, and 0.90 still preserved full resolution with only a modest time penalty. Testing phi1 0.85 will show whether the late hold strength can be reduced further while maintaining adequate separation, completing a useful map of the only major composition axis not yet bracketed.

The endpoint trend is now consistent: lowering phi1 increases retention while preserving resolution, so one more step to 0.80 will finish that map and confirm there is no hidden selectivity gain worth trading for time. This is the most informative unused neighbor along the remaining composition axis around the known optimum.

The best method sits right at the boundary where shortening from 18 to 16 min caused only a small resolution loss, so the steepness limit in tG is the remaining key local variable. Testing 14 min will define the lower gradient-time boundary and fully bracket the optimum along the most sensitive axis.

The tG and phi0 trends indicate the optimum is near the boundary between faster gradients and loss of resolution, so combining the safer lower phi0 with the shorter 16 min gradient is the most plausible unexplored route to recover full resolution while keeping zero time penalty. This directly tests whether a modest reduction in starting strength can rescue the critical pair that failed at phi0 0.20, tG 16.

We now have two max-CRF points, so the key remaining question is how far the faster/lower-phi0 tradeoff can be pushed before the critical pair fails. Shortening the new successful phi0 0.15 method to 14 min directly tests whether there is an even broader 1.000 plateau on the fast side.

The two 1.000 methods suggest a ridge where lower phi0 can compensate for shorter tG, so stepping phi0 down again at 16 min is the most informative unexplored point on that ridge. This tests whether the max-CRF plateau extends further toward gentler starting conditions with added resolution margin.

The explored 1.000 ridge suggests decreasing phi0 restores resolution as tG shortens, so the next logical point is phi0 0.10 at 14 min. This directly tests whether that ridge extends to another max-CRF condition or breaks between the successful 0.15/16 and the failing shorter, stronger-start methods.

The remaining unexplored point on the apparent phi0–tG tradeoff ridge is phi0 0.05 at 16 min, which should add resolution margin while staying close to the zero-time-penalty region. This completes the local map and tests whether the 1.000 plateau extends to the gentlest start at this shorter gradient time.

With the optimum already found, the last unused high-information corner near the fast/strong-start region is to combine the stronger phi0 with the hot condition that partly recovered from the 45 C selectivity collapse. This final run probes whether the critical-pair identities can reshuffle into a different local optimum, while all simpler neighborhoods around the max-CRF methods are already well mapped.
